generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, a good presentation is planned before any slide is made. You read the brief and marking criteria, gather your evidence, and decide the one message you want the audience to leave with. Then you set a shape: an introduction that frames the question, a main body that works through the evidence in order, and a conclusion that states what it shows. This structure helps an audience follow an argument built on studies and data.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students prepare the same ten-minute presentation on a study.

Tom opens the slide software straight away and starts making slides. Points about the method, the results and his own views go in as they come to mind, with no clear order and no single message. The result is a set of slides that jump about, and a talk the audience cannot follow. Tom skipped the planning, so the presentation has no shape.

Amara plans first. She reads the brief, gathers her evidence, then decides on one main message and the order of her points. Only then does she make the slides. Her talk opens with an introduction, develops the evidence in the main body, and ends with a conclusion. She practises it once to check the timing. The audience can follow it easily.

Both had the same time to prepare. Only Amara planned and structured the presentation before building the slides.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, a presentation is put together in steps: understand the brief, research, plan, design the visual aids, and practise. Planning is where you set the structure, and most presentations share a three-part shape of introduction, main body and conclusion. You can now describe the steps in preparing a presentation, identify its three parts, and choose a sound planning move. The next lesson turns to the visual aids themselves, and the errors to avoid.

check.body: In the worked example, how did Amara give her talk a shape that Tom's lacked?

items.text: She opened with an introduction, developed her evidence in a main body, and ended with a conclusion.
She used more slides than Tom did.
She spoke faster so she could fit everything in.
She added her points in the order they came to mind.

feedback.correct: That's right. The introduction, main body and conclusion gave Amara's talk a shape Tom's lacked.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about the three-part shape Amara planned before making slides.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara gave her talk an introduction, a main body and a conclusion. More slides, speaking faster or adding points at random do not give a talk its shape.
